content: Sudden cardiac death (SCD) is defined as an unexpected death occurring within one hour of the onset of symptoms, attributed to cardiac causes, and typically confirmed through post-mortem examination. It is a leading cause of mortality in Western countries, accounting for 15-20% of all deaths. Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the most common underlying pathology associated with SCD. Advances in medical treatment and prevention of CAD have led to a decline in the incidence of both CAD and SCD. However, further research is necessary to better understand the mechanisms underlying this condition. Historically, SCD occurs abruptly and unexpectedly in individuals without known cardiac disease, typically within one hour of symptom onset. Approximately 25% of human deaths are attributed to SCD, with ventricular fibrillation (VF) being the most common mechanism. The concept of SCD was first proposed by MacWilliam over 120 years ago, before the invention of the electrocardiogram (ECG). Sudden cardiac arrest refers to the abrupt cessation of cardiac activity, resulting in an unresponsive patient with gasping respiration or no respiratory movement and unpalpable pulses due to cardiac causes such as arrhythmia or pump failure. Aborted cardiac arrest is described as a reversible, unexpected circulatory collapse within one hour of symptom onset, following successful cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) is a sudden death in infants with a structurally normal heart and no specific findings on autopsy or toxicology. The pathophysiology of cardiac arrest involves myocardial inflammation in the context of atherosclerosis, structural heart disease, genetic disorders, and environmental factors. Mutations in genes such as SCN5A, KCNH2, KCNQ1, RYR2, MYBPC3, PKP2, and DSP are associated with inherited causes of cardiac arrest and SCD. Sudden cardiac arrest can result from various causes, including coronary artery abnormalities (e.g., coronary atherosclerosis, acute myocardial infarction, coronary artery embolism, or arteritis), myocardial hypertrophy (e.g., hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hypertensive heart disease), pulmonary hypertension, myocardial diseases (e.g., ischemic or non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, myocarditis), valvular heart disease (e.g., aortic stenosis, mitral valve prolapse), congenital heart defects (e.g., septal defects with Eisenmenger physiology), conduction system abnormalities (e.g., Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome), and electrical instability (e.g., catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, long QT syndrome). Following an initial diagnosis of cardiac arrest, healthcare professionals categorize the condition based on the presenting ECG rhythm. There are four rhythms associated with cardiac arrest: ventricular fibrillation (VF) and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT), which are shockable rhythms responsive to defibrillation, and asystole and pulseless electrical activity (PEA), which are non-shockable rhythms. The presenting rhythm provides insight into the underlying cause and guides treatment decisions. Epidemiologically, SCD accounts for nearly 50% of all cardiovascular-related deaths. Its incidence increases with age, and men are more commonly affected than women across all age groups. Racial and ethnic backgrounds also influence the risk of SCD. Risk factors for SCD include hypertension, male gender, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, obesity, smoking, older age, obstructive sleep apnea (due to hypoxia), early VF (within 48 hours of acute coronary syndrome, increasing in-hospital mortality fivefold), early repolarization patterns during myocardial infarction, and a family history of sudden death. Screening for SCD should focus on identifying individuals with risk factors associated with the condition. The natural history of sudden cardiac arrest involves a sudden disruption in cardiac electrical propagation or the heart's inability to pump blood effectively to vital organs. Early clinical features include abrupt palpitations, presyncope, syncope, chest pain, dyspnea, and hypotension within one hour before the terminal event. Patients may progress to cardiac arrest, characterized by sudden collapse, loss of effective circulation, and loss of consciousness. Without treatment or successful resuscitation, biological death can occur within minutes to weeks. In-hospital cardiac deaths are often due to multiorgan dysfunction, with one-fourth resulting from neurological complications. Poor prognostic factors include age over 70, underlying disorders (e.g., pneumonia, hypotension, renal or hepatic dysfunction), and non-shockable rhythms (e.g., asystole, PEA). Better prognostic factors include early detection or witnessed arrest, shockable rhythms (e.g., VF, VT), and female gender between 15-45 years of age. In-hospital cardiac arrest generally has a better prognosis than out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, with a one-year survival rate of approximately 25% for patients discharged from the hospital. Symptoms preceding cardiac arrest may include palpitations, lightheadedness, syncope, dyspnea at rest or with exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, chest pain, and edema. Physical examination of patients in cardiac arrest often reveals cyanosis. Findings may include abnormalities in heart rate and rhythm, blood pressure, jugular venous pressure, murmurs, pulses, bruits, edema, or sternotomy scars. Laboratory findings, such as elevated brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) levels, may predict ventricular arrhythmias and SCD. An ECG can aid in diagnosing SCD. Common findings include sinus tachycardia, abnormal T-wave inversions, prolonged QT intervals, atrial abnormalities, left ventricular hypertrophy, abnormal QRS axis, delayed QRS transition zones, pathological Q waves, intraventricular conduction delays, multiple premature ventricular contractions, or a normal ECG. Chest X-rays may help identify underlying causes of cardiac arrest, such as cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema, massive pericardial effusion, or a widened aortic silhouette. Echocardiography can assist in diagnosing the cause of lethal arrhythmias and cardiac arrest by evaluating regional wall motion abnormalities, left ventricular systolic function, evidence of myocardial infarction, valvular heart disease, right ventricular cardiomyopathy, pericardial effusion, tamponade, or aortic dissection. Cardiac CT scans can evaluate left ventricular volumes, ejection fraction, cardiac masses, anomalous coronary artery origins, coronary artery calcifications, pulmonary embolism, or aortic dissection. Cardiac MRI is a precise modality for diagnosing structural and functional causes of cardiac arrest by assessing chamber volumes, left ventricular mass, size, and function, right ventricular size and function, and regional wall motion abnormalities. For survivors of SCD due to ischemic heart disease, coronary angiography and potential revascularization are recommended. Electrophysiology studies may be used to induce arrhythmias and determine the need for implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) placement in conditions such as dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC), or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). However, electrophysiology studies are not recommended for long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, or short QT syndrome. Management of cardiac arrest involves immediate rhythm assessment. VF or pulseless VT requires immediate defibrillation, while asystole or PEA necessitates resumption of CPR. Advanced life support (ALS) should minimize interruptions in chest compressions and include advanced airway management, continuous chest compressions, capnography, IV/IO access, vasopressors, antiarrhythmic therapy, and correction of reversible causes (e.g., hypoxia, hypovolemia, hypothermia, hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, acidosis, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins). Post-arrest care focuses on treating the underlying disorder, maintaining hemodynamic stability, providing respiratory support, and managing neurological complications. Primary prevention of SCD in at-risk individuals includes ICD implantation based on guidelines. Secondary prevention strategies after aborted SCD include revascularization in ischemic heart disease and ICD placement in patients with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction and a history of lethal arrhythmias. Post-STEMI patients should receive evidence-based therapies, such as beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors (or ARBs for ACEI-intolerant patients), and statins. Aldosterone antagonists may be added for symptomatic congestive heart failure. Antiarrhythmics like amiodarone and sotalol do not reduce all-cause mortality post-STEMI but may reduce ICD shocks in patients with high shock rates. ICD placement is indicated for patients with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction 40 days post-MI or three months post-revascularization. Ethical considerations include recognizing that CPR and advanced cardiac life support may not always be in a patient’s best interest, particularly in terminal illnesses where resuscitation will not alter the disease outcome. Properly performed CPR can cause rib fractures, especially in older patients or those with osteoporosis, and repeated defibrillation may cause electrical burns. Patients with terminal illnesses may choose to forgo such measures and opt for a peaceful death. Patients should discuss their preferences with their doctor and family and may request a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order or document their wishes in an advance directive.
